lessons.title: Find the person who uses the forecast
lessons.why_this_step: A useful forecast arrives while someone can still act on it. Start with the person who makes the decision and the situation in which they make it.
how_to_do_it: Name the person or role that will read the forecast.
Ask when they make the decision and what they look at today.
Describe the constraints they face when they act.
lessons.how_to_read: Check that a colleague could identify the recipient, the moment of use and the action they control from the description.
pitfalls: Naming a whole department hides responsibility. In a walkthrough, nobody can say who would receive the forecast or respond to it.
A forecast can arrive too late. When you replay a typical decision, the recipient has already committed to an action.
lessons.question: Who can still act when the forecast arrives?

illustration.caption: Start with a person and an action. Use those to decide what the forecast should report.

lessons.title: Connect the forecast to a decision
lessons.why_this_step: A forecast matters when different values can lead to different actions. Naming the decision gives you a way to judge whether better predictions would help.
how_to_do_it: Write down the action the person takes today.
Describe an alternative action they can actually take.
Ask which forecast values would make them choose the alternative.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the proposed use as a pair of examples. Each gives a possible forecast and the action it would support.
pitfalls: A forecast can be interesting yet unused. When you try plausible low and high values, the intended user makes the same choice each time.
An option can be impractical. The walkthrough reaches a proposed action that exceeds the team's capacity or authority.
lessons.question: Which plausible forecast would make the person change their action?

lessons.title: Fix the time when you predict
lessons.why_this_step: Prediction time determines what information can be used. A clear cutoff makes a historical evaluation represent the conditions in which a forecast will be made.
how_to_do_it: Place the forecast on the timeline of the decision.
Declare the latest time at which inputs may become available.
Replay a past forecast with only the information that existed at the cutoff.
lessons.how_to_read: Compare each input's availability time with the cutoff. An event timestamp describes when an event happened. A delivery timestamp describes when you could use its data.
pitfalls: Late data can make a historical forecast too strong. The replay includes a value posted after the declared cutoff.
lessons.question: What would you actually know if you had to predict at the cutoff?

illustration.caption: Use only inputs available by the cutoff. Use the later outcome to judge the prediction.

lessons.title: Set the horizon and the outcome cutoff
lessons.why_this_step: The horizon defines the future window the forecast covers. Outcome maturity tells you when the observed value is complete enough to use for evaluation.
how_to_do_it: Write when the outcome window opens and closes relative to prediction time.
Find when outcomes for that window become complete in the source.
Exclude outcomes that could still change when you assemble the evaluation.
lessons.how_to_read: Read prediction time, window end and outcome maturity as successive moments. A record may be present while its outcome is still incomplete.
pitfalls: Treating recent outcomes as final biases the evaluation. The same units acquire more events when you refresh the data.
A shifted outcome window changes the question. A timeline check finds a forecast scored on a period other than the one it names.
lessons.question: How long after the outcome window closes can you trust the observed value?

lessons.title: Define what one forecast is about
lessons.why_this_step: The unit tells you which prediction should match which outcome. It also determines which errors count once when you summarise performance.
how_to_do_it: Describe one forecast as a named entity over a stated time window.
Choose a key that identifies that unit on both sides of the evaluation.
Check for duplicate keys and missing matches before calculating errors.
lessons.how_to_read: Read one joined row aloud as a sentence about the entity and its time window. Each forecast should match the outcome for that same unit.
pitfalls: A duplicated key overweights some units. The joined table grows when it should keep a single match for each forecast.
Different time windows make errors hard to interpret. A sample row pairs a forecast and outcome that cover different periods.
lessons.question: What entity and time window does a single forecast describe?

lessons.title: Choose a Metric that reflects the decision
lessons.why_this_step: A Metric converts errors into a measure you can compare. It should reflect the mistakes the intended user most needs to avoid.
how_to_do_it: List the consequences of predicting too high and too low.
Select a Metric whose treatment of those mistakes matches the intended use.
State the unit, the direction of improvement and how units are combined.
lessons.how_to_read: Translate an error into something the recipient recognises. Check how the Metric responds when a large error or a systematic bias appears.
pitfalls: A convenient Metric can reward forecasts that make the wrong tradeoff. Two example errors have similar scores even though one leads to a much more costly decision.
An average can conceal a recurring problem. Overall error falls while errors grow during the period when the recipient depends on the forecast.
lessons.question: Which forecasting mistake should this Metric penalise most?

lessons.title: Set the smallest useful improvement
lessons.why_this_step: A measured gain can be too small to justify changing a working process. A threshold in the Metric's unit connects the result to what the recipient can use.
how_to_do_it: Ask what change in forecast error would affect an action or its cost.
Translate that change into the Metric's unit.
Write down how you will handle an interval that crosses the threshold.
lessons.how_to_read: Compare the estimated improvement and its interval with the threshold. If the interval spans it, the evidence leaves open whether the gain is large enough to matter.
pitfalls: A threshold picked after seeing results can favour the Candidate. The recorded threshold first appears after someone has examined the Comparison.
A threshold in the wrong unit invites a false comparison. The rule gives a proportion while the Comparison gives an absolute error difference.
lessons.question: What smallest improvement would make switching worthwhile?

lessons.title: Record the decision rule before seeing results
lessons.why_this_step: An advance record makes it possible to tell which evidence the choice was meant to use. It keeps an appealing result from silently changing the terms of the decision.
how_to_do_it: Write the Control, Metric, minimum useful difference and decision conditions.
State what you will do when the evidence is inconclusive.
Record the rule as a Decision before the first Exposure.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the recorded rule as instructions another person could apply. They should be able to tell when to keep the Control, choose the Candidate or defer the choice.
pitfalls: A vague rule lets two people make different choices from the same evidence. A walkthrough reaches a case for which the rule gives no outcome.
A later edit can hide a change of mind. The Study has a result under one rule but the written rationale silently applies a different one.
lessons.question: Could someone apply your rule to an inconclusive result without asking you to fill in a condition?

lessons.title: Check when each feature becomes available
lessons.why_this_step: A feature can describe the past and still arrive after prediction time. The model can rely on it only if the value is available when the forecast is due.
how_to_do_it: List each feature's source, event time and first availability time.
Rebuild a sample of past inputs using the versions available at each cutoff.
Remove features that arrive late or replace them with values available by the cutoff.
lessons.how_to_read: Read availability as a timeline. A daily total may carry the date it describes while becoming usable only when the source publishes it.
pitfalls: A revised value can leak later information. The historical extract differs from the version published at prediction time.
A feature can arrive late only on some days. A cutoff replay shows gaps even though the latest extract has complete coverage.
lessons.question: Which feature would disappear first if you rebuilt the data as it looked at each cutoff?

illustration.caption: The early feature is available for this forecast. The daily total belongs to a later forecast.

lessons.title: Inspect the inputs before using outcomes
lessons.why_this_step: Input checks can expose collection and join problems before the outcome influences what you fix. Start with properties you could inspect at prediction time.
how_to_do_it: Summarise missing inputs, duplicate keys and time coverage.
Compare those summaries across relevant sources and periods.
Record each exclusion rule and the input condition that triggers it.
lessons.how_to_read: Read missingness by period and source. A normal overall rate can hide a complete outage in one period or repeated rows from a broken join.
pitfalls: Dropping units after seeing their outcomes can improve the score artificially. The exclusion rule refers to error or outcome values unavailable at the cutoff.
A global summary can conceal a collection failure. A breakdown shows one source contributes almost no usable rows during an important period.
lessons.question: Which input problem could leave the overall missingness rate looking acceptable?

lessons.title: Understand what outcomes are common
lessons.why_this_step: A forecast can look accurate when it handles common outcomes and misses the ones that matter. The distribution tells you what the baseline must account for.
how_to_do_it: Summarise the training outcomes in their natural units.
Compare typical values and extreme values across relevant time periods.
Check how often a decision-relevant outcome occurs when the decision uses a threshold.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the centre, spread and tails together. If the decision depends on a threshold, the share above it gives the base rate for that event.
pitfalls: A single average can hide seasonality or rare extremes. Summaries by period reveal a range the overall average misses.
A good score can come from predicting the common outcome. The baseline matches the overall score while forecasts miss the events that trigger action.
lessons.question: Which rare outcome matters enough to check separately?

lessons.title: Separate earlier training from later evaluation
lessons.why_this_step: A temporal split tests predictions on a later period, where data and conditions can change. It also makes the timing of feature fitting and outcome maturity visible.
how_to_do_it: Order units by prediction time before assigning Partitions.
Reserve a later period for development evaluation.
Check that training outcomes are mature before the first prediction in the later period.
Fit transformations using only the training data available at each cutoff.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the split on a timeline. Trace a row near the boundary from its prediction time through its outcome window and the day that outcome became available.
pitfalls: Overlapping outcome windows can bring later information into training. A boundary check finds a training outcome that was still incomplete when later forecasts begin.
A preprocessing step can use the whole dataset. Its fitted summaries include rows beyond the training boundary.
lessons.question: Which training row near the boundary might still have an unfinished outcome?

lessons.title: Investigate signs of leakage
lessons.why_this_step: A dramatic gain can come from information unavailable when you predict. An investigation should trace the gain to specific data or operations that you can verify.
how_to_do_it: List inputs or transformations that could use future information.
Rebuild the suspect part using only what was available when each prediction was made.
Compare the result with the same baseline under the original split and Metric.
lessons.how_to_read: Treat a sharp score change as a clue. Trace the input's availability and the operation's fit window before drawing a conclusion.
pitfalls: A changed split can mimic the effect of removing leakage. The new run changes both the suspected input and the period being scored.
A timestamp check can accept a revised value as historical. A recorded snapshot at the cutoff contains a different version.
lessons.question: Which input or transformation would you audit first if an unexpectedly large gain appeared?

lessons.title: Build a simple forecast to beat
lessons.why_this_step: A simple forecast establishes how much value a more complex approach adds to patterns that are already easy to exploit.
how_to_do_it: Choose a rule that uses information available at prediction time, such as the last available observation for the same weekday.
Fix the rule and its fallback for missing history before scoring.
Score the rule on the same units, horizon and Metric planned for the Candidate.
lessons.how_to_read: Use the baseline result to judge improvement. A baseline that performs well can expose a Candidate that adds complexity for little gain.
pitfalls: Using the last recorded observation instead of the last available one leaks information. The source first published it after the forecast was issued.
Dropping units without history makes the baseline look stronger. The covered units or the number of forecasts differ from the Candidate.
lessons.question: What simple rule could someone apply using only information available when the forecast is issued?

illustration.caption: Build a baseline from information that would really be available. Score it under the Candidate's Protocol.

lessons.title: Use the current pipeline as the Control
lessons.why_this_step: The existing pipeline represents the choice the user can keep. Replaying it fairly measures what replacing it would change.
how_to_do_it: Freeze the current pipeline and its settings before evaluating variants.
Reproduce the inputs, forecast timing and fallback behavior it would have used on each evaluation unit.
Score the Control and Candidate under the same Protocol.
lessons.how_to_read: Check that the replay is representative of the current service. A good result against a simplified substitute gives weaker evidence for replacement.
pitfalls: Reconstructing inputs from today's corrected data can distort the replay. Archived inputs differ from the values used in the replay.
Updating the Control during iteration shifts the comparison. The recorded Control changes between otherwise similar Assessments.
lessons.question: Which part of the current pipeline would be hardest to reproduce as it ran at the time?

lessons.title: Probe for shortcuts with shuffled targets
lessons.why_this_step: A deliberately broken training signal can expose a pipeline that still learns from information it should be unable to see.
how_to_do_it: Shuffle the training targets within a justified scheme that breaks the predictor and target association being tested.
Repeat the training and feature building steps with those targets while preserving the forecast timing and splits.
Score on the original validation targets and compare the result with the simple baseline.
lessons.how_to_read: A surprising gain after shuffling calls for an audit. Consider what seasonal or group structure the shuffle preserves before interpreting the result.
pitfalls: A stale cache can make the shuffle probe train against the original labels. The target table used for fitting still matches the unshuffled values.
Allowing nearby observations to cross the split can preserve dependence. The apparent gain shrinks when the split respects time and label availability.
lessons.question: What relationship does your shuffle break, and what structure does it preserve?

lessons.title: Give each variant one question
lessons.why_this_step: A focused change makes the result easier to interpret and gives the next variant a purpose.
how_to_do_it: State the uncertainty the variant will address and the finding you expect.
Change the smallest part of the Configuration that can answer the question.
Hold the Protocol and Control fixed, then record the result against the original expectation.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the result as evidence about the stated change under this Protocol. Coupled changes can still answer a question if they are explicitly evaluated as a package.
pitfalls: Changing features, tuning and the evaluation window together hides the cause. A gain appears, but the records cannot attribute it to any one change.
Writing the question after scoring disguises an exploratory result as a prediction. The expectation has no record from before the Attempt.
lessons.question: What is the smallest change that would help you answer your question?

illustration.caption: Use the same Protocol on both sides. A comparison of one change gives you a clearer next question.

lessons.title: Set an Attempt budget before iteration
lessons.why_this_step: Repeated choices based on dev results can fit the evaluation window itself. An Attempt budget preserves the value of the evidence for choosing.
how_to_do_it: Set an Attempt budget and a stopping rule before examining variant results.
Keep a record of each dev result that could influence the next choice.
Use the remaining budget for questions whose answers could change the Decision.
lessons.how_to_read: Treat a late dev gain in light of how many tries informed it. Look for a reason the change should help beyond the exact window already inspected.
pitfalls: Repeatedly trying variations can select a lucky result. The strongest score follows many near-identical attempts with mixed outcomes.
Restarting the tally after a small change hides prior feedback. The variant history shows more dev-informed choices than the current budget records.
lessons.question: What result would make further dev Attempts unlikely to change your Decision?

lessons.title: Validate inside the training window
lessons.why_this_step: Internal time-ordered validation lets you tune choices while keeping dev feedback for the decisions it was reserved to support.
how_to_do_it: Place successive fit and validation windows within the original training period.
Fit preprocessing and the model using only data and mature labels available at each cutoff.
Choose settings from those internal runs and fit the selected Configuration on the eligible training data.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the variation across cutoffs alongside the average score. A setting that helps only at one cutoff has weaker evidence than one that helps across times.
pitfalls: Fitting transformations before splitting passes information backwards. Validation features change when later rows are removed.
Including labels that mature after the cutoff gives the fit future knowledge. Their observation times precede the cutoff but their availability times follow it.
lessons.question: At a given validation cutoff, which training labels would still be unavailable?

lessons.title: Find patterns in forecast errors
lessons.why_this_step: A single score can hide systematic misses at times when users rely on the forecast most.
how_to_do_it: Define the residual sign and group the errors using conditions available when forecasts were issued.
Compare errors across time and across groups tied to the user's Decision.
Check how many observations support each pattern and inspect whether it persists across periods.
lessons.how_to_read: Read positive and negative residuals according to your sign convention. Look for repeated direction or scale within a group before proposing a change.
pitfalls: Averaging signed residuals can hide large errors that cancel out. The average is near zero while absolute errors remain large.
Searching many small groups can make noise look persistent. The pattern depends on a few observations or disappears in the next window.
lessons.question: Which recurring error would cause the most trouble for the person using the forecast?

lessons.title: Check what forecast values and ranges promise
lessons.why_this_step: Forecasts used to plan for risk need a reliable relationship between what they predict and what is observed.
how_to_do_it: Group point forecasts into meaningful ranges and compare their average values with the average outcomes.
Check observed coverage against the intended coverage when the pipeline also supplies prediction intervals.
Repeat the check across important operating periods with enough observations to interpret the result.
lessons.how_to_read: Look for systematic bias across point forecast ranges. For intervals, read coverage together with width. Very wide intervals may cover often while giving little guidance.
pitfalls: Overall coverage can hide undercoverage when risk is highest. Misses concentrate in a busy period despite acceptable total coverage.
Using the same outcomes to fit a correction and check it makes the correction look more reliable. The gain shrinks at a later evaluation cutoff.
lessons.question: Where would a biased point forecast or an overconfident range change the action someone takes?

lessons.title: Relate the paired delta to the decision
lessons.why_this_step: A paired delta measures a change on shared evaluation units. Its sign matters only when you know the subtraction order and the Metric direction.
how_to_do_it: Identify the Candidate, the Control and the direction in which the Metric improves.
Confirm that the Comparison pairs outcomes from the same units under the same Protocol.
Translate the direction and size of the reported delta into what it would change for the user.
lessons.how_to_read: Read the delta in the Metric's units. If it subtracts Control error from Candidate error, a positive delta means the Candidate error is larger.
pitfalls: Switching the subtraction order reverses the interpretation. The written winner disagrees with the two scores and the stated formula.
Reading an aggregate gain as a gain for every group overstates the evidence. A group relevant to the user has little evidence of improvement.
lessons.question: Given the subtraction order and Metric, which side of zero would support the Candidate?

lessons.title: Read the interval against your decision rule
lessons.why_this_step: An interval describes uncertainty around the estimated gap. The decision rule sets the size of gap that matters in practice.
how_to_do_it: Check the interval method and any dependence assumptions for repeated or nearby observations.
Put zero and the minimum useful improvement on the delta scale using the subtraction order and the direction of improvement.
Compare both bounds with those values and apply the rule stated before evaluation.
lessons.how_to_read: An interval that crosses zero leaves both directions compatible with the estimate and method. An interval on the improvement side can still include gaps too small to act on.
pitfalls: Reporting the point estimate alone conceals uncertainty. The preferred option changes when you apply the rule to the interval bounds.
Treating nearby observations as independent can produce an interval that is too narrow. Nearby forecast errors tend to move together.
lessons.question: Which uncertainty matters for your choice, the direction of the effect or whether it is large enough?

illustration.caption: Put the rule and the interval on the same signed scale before interpreting the evidence.

lessons.title: Check whether the Comparison supports the claim
lessons.why_this_step: A number can describe the wrong contrast when the two sides differ in coverage, scoring or what they could know at prediction time.
how_to_do_it: Check the units, horizon, Metric, eligibility and pairing for both sides.
Read each warning or limitation before interpreting the delta.
Narrow the claim or defer the choice when a limitation prevents a fair answer to the original question.
lessons.how_to_read: Distinguish a limitation that narrows who the result applies to from one that makes the contrast unreliable. Keep any resulting restriction with the Decision.
pitfalls: Ignoring missing pairs can overstate gain. The usable units leave out part of the time range that motivated the change.
Interpreting a withheld delta as zero suggests equality. The panel instead shows a warning or an unavailable result.
lessons.question: Which assumption would have to hold before you could act on this Comparison?

lessons.title: Record the decision in your own words
lessons.why_this_step: The next person needs to see the choice you made, the evidence you relied on and the conditions under which you would reopen it.
how_to_do_it: State what you choose and link your reason to the Comparison.
Explain any uncertainty or limitation that affects the choice.
Review the wording in the panel and use Record when it says what you intend.
lessons.how_to_read: A clear Decision identifies the action and explains how the evidence supports it. Someone returning later can tell whether new evidence changes the reason.
pitfalls: Accepting wording you would not use can hide an important qualification. On rereading it, it promises more than you meant.
Writing only that the score improved makes the Decision hard to revisit. The reason gives no Metric direction, practical threshold or meaningful limitation.
lessons.question: What finding would make you reopen this Decision?

lessons.title: Hand over the forecast and its limits
lessons.why_this_step: A handover makes the forecast usable and lets someone reconstruct the evidence behind the Decision.
how_to_do_it: Describe who will act on the forecast, when it is issued and where the result is delivered.
Document the exact Configuration, input expectations, fallback behavior and Decision rationale.
Give the recipient a way to reproduce the run and to find the relevant Study records.
lessons.how_to_read: Ask whether a recipient can operate the forecast, recognise a case outside its scope and explain why this Configuration was chosen.
pitfalls: Leaving out the fallback causes silent failures. The recipient has no usable procedure when an input arrives late.
Sharing only a summary score loses the decision trail. A recipient cannot find the Comparison, the Configuration or the limitations behind the choice.
lessons.question: Could the recipient run the forecast and recognise when to fall back without asking you?

illustration.caption: Give the next reader enough context to apply the Decision and recognise when it needs another Study.

lessons.title: Monitor what can change the decision
lessons.why_this_step: Forecasts can become less useful as inputs, operating conditions or the time at which labels arrive change.
how_to_do_it: Name the input freshness, forecast coverage and outcome measures that matter for the intended use.
Assign responsibility for observing those measures and acting when a review condition is met.
Plan an early input check and a later error check when outcomes have matured.
lessons.how_to_read: Read input health and mature-outcome performance together. Healthy inputs can coexist with worse forecasts if the relationship to the outcome has changed.
pitfalls: Counting incomplete outcomes as if they were complete distorts reported performance. Recent periods contain more missing labels.
Tracking only the overall error hides a failure that matters to one operating group. Group-level misses increase while the headline score appears stable.
lessons.question: Which signal would tell you to act before the outcome labels arrive?

lessons.title: Plan the next cycle around a new question
lessons.why_this_step: A new cycle should address what the last Decision left uncertain or what monitoring shows has changed.
how_to_do_it: Write the new question and identify the observation that raised it.
Choose fresh evaluation evidence and state how earlier results will inform the design.
Set a new decision rule and budget before using the new dev feedback.
lessons.how_to_read: Keep the previous Decision as a record of what the evidence supported then. Explain which new conditions or findings would justify a different choice.
pitfalls: Stretching the old conclusion into a new setting hides a change in scope. The next users, forecast timing or outcome differ from the prior Protocol.
Reusing repeatedly inspected data as independent evidence exaggerates confidence. The new choices were already informed by the same outcomes.
lessons.question: What has changed since the last Decision that the next cycle ought to test?
